tldr: This paper presents a method for real-time, high-precision drift control under extreme conditions where tires slide sideways, combining flow models (generative AI) with reinforcement learning. Demonstrating strong robustness whether trained from scratch or fine-tuned from expert demonstrations, the policy achieves a 100% success rate even under severe disturbances.
hero_caption: A 3-DoF vehicle dynamics model for a rear-wheel-drive small RC car (F1TENTH). It models trajectory tracking at handling limits by accounting for vehicle sideslip angle, yaw rate, and nonlinear tire lateral forces.
overview:
In emergency obstacle avoidance or driving on snow and low-friction surfaces, the ability to skillfully control and recover a vehicle in its handling limits (a drifting state)—where it is close to spinning out—is essential. However, during drifting, tire grip reaches its limit, lateral forces saturate, and vehicle behavior exhibits severe non-linearity. Conventional Model Predictive Control (MPC) requires an accurate vehicle model and imposes heavy computational loads on onboard microcontrollers. Meanwhile, standard reinforcement learning (RL) struggles because even a minor control error leads to spinning out, making exploration of effective actions exceptionally difficult.

To tackle this, the authors devised an approach combining generative policies based on "flow matching"—popularized in image generation—with online reinforcement learning. Along with the flexible action representation typical of generative models, the system employs stochastic differential equation (SDE) noise sampling for exploration during training, switching to fast ordinary differential equation (ODE) integration to determine actions during inference. Furthermore, by introducing a surrogate entropy metric easily computed from SDE transition probabilities rather than intractable exact action entropy, they enable adaptive control over exploration noise scale.

Evaluations were conducted on an F1TENTH digital twin platform at physical scale, testing circular drifting and more challenging figure-eight drifting. Results show that both training from scratch without expert data and fine-tuning from expert demonstrations rapidly acquire stable drifting.

The robustness against disturbances is particularly striking. Despite being trained exclusively on the nominal model (without noise), the proposed method maintained a 100% success rate in a harsh environment (S5) featuring initial state errors, variations in vehicle mass and tire friction, and strong disturbance noise, whereas the baseline model-based controller dropped to a 25% success rate. With an inference latency of just 0.5 ms, it proves fast enough for practical deployment on embedded hardware.
contributions: Proposed an autonomous drifting control framework that optimizes flow matching-based generative policies via online reinforcement learning.
Achieved efficient action exploration during training using stochastic differential equations (SDEs), combined with adaptive noise scaling and a computationally tractable surrogate entropy metric.
Demonstrated the flexibility to acquire challenging drifting behaviors both through fine-tuning from expert data and training from scratch.
Demonstrated strong robustness by maintaining a 100% success rate and high tracking accuracy under harsh disturbances and vehicle parameter variations, despite training solely on the nominal model.

sections.heading: Evolution from Model-Based Control to Generative AI Policies
sections.summary: While conventional autonomous drift control has centered on model-based methods like MPC, computational cost and vulnerability to model mismatches have remained challenges. Building on recent advances in RL and generative modeling, this study provides a new learning framework balancing data efficiency with real-time capability.
sections.details:
### Model-Based Drift Control
Conventional drift control has widely relied on inverse-model control based on error dynamics or Model Predictive Control (MPC). In particular, nonlinear MPC has a proven track record for drift tracking in real vehicles. However, it requires solving an optimization problem online continuously, demanding specialized solver design and deep expertise to run in real time on embedded hardware. The HDDC controller used as a baseline in this paper is an excellent model-based technique offering clear physical control intuition, yet it remains sensitive to modeling errors.

### Reinforcement Learning in Drift Control
Reinforcement learning (RL), which learns control policies directly through trial-and-error interaction with the environment, has also been studied. Methods based on Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) or PPO have explored incorporating human drift driving data or leveraging large-scale parallel simulations. However, because drifting demands tight coordination between throttle and steering, losing control results in meaningless experience, turning massive trial data consumption into a bottleneck.

### Rise of Generative Policies
"Generative policies" that apply diffusion models (Diffusion Policy) or flow matching to robotic action generation are advancing rapidly. Their primary strength lies in representing complex, multimodal action distributions. While recent work has expanded beyond imitation learning into offline-to-online RL, many prior methods still rely on deterministic ODE sampling, limiting effective online exploration. This work distinguishes itself by systematically incorporating SDE-based sampling into online RL for active exploration.

sections.heading: Capturing Drift via Mechanics: Vehicle Modeling and Expert Design
sections.summary: Targeting a rear-wheel-drive scale vehicle, the authors define 3-DoF equations of motion incorporating the Fiala brush tire model to express lateral force saturation. They also derive reference trajectories from drift equilibria and establish an expert controller (HDDC) pipeline to collect initial offline data.
sections.details:
### III-A Vehicle and Tire Modeling
The target platform is a rear-wheel-drive (RWD) F1TENTH race car. The paper adopts a 3-degree-of-freedom (3-DoF) single-track bicycle model accounting for two translational motions and one rotational yaw motion. The state variables include vehicle sideslip angle $\beta$, yaw rate $r$, and center-of-mass velocity $v$, with steering angle $\delta$ and rear longitudinal driving force $F_{xr}$ serving as control inputs.

To compute tire lateral forces, the model uses the Fiala brush tire model, which faithfully captures behavior at physical limits. While tire slip angle $\alpha$ remains small, lateral force increases linearly; once it exceeds the limit angle, grip saturates and transitions into sliding. Because the rear tires are constrained by friction circle limits coupling longitudinal and lateral forces, applying throttle reduces available lateral grip—accurately modeling the tight, nonlinear coupling unique to drifting.

### III-A3 Reference Trajectory Design via Equilibrium Analysis
A steady-state drift corresponds to a dynamic equilibrium where rates of change in sideslip angle and yaw rate are zero ($\dot{\beta}=\dot{r}=\dot{v}=0$). By specifying the ideal velocity and sideslip angle at each waypoint along the target trajectory and solving the vehicle equations, the required yaw rate, steering angle, and longitudinal drive force are uniquely determined. Mechanically, this equilibrium lies near a saddle point, representing an extremely unstable state that diverges easily under minor disturbances.

### III-B Expert Demonstration Collection
Transitions are collected for offline learning by running the model-based HDDC controller. The observation vector $\bm{o_t}$ includes vehicle position, heading, velocity, and tracking errors relative to the reference path (cross-track error $e_d$, heading error $e_\theta$, sideslip error $e_\beta$, etc.). The input $\bm{s_t}$ to the policy concatenates these observations across the past 9 time steps. Adding moderate noise to the state variables during collection ensures data diversity.

sections.heading: Unifying Flow Matching and RL: SDE Exploration and Fast Inference
sections.summary: The authors construct a flow model generating actions via continuous vector fields and integrate it with Actor-Critic learning. Training utilizes SDE sampling and a tractable surrogate entropy metric for active exploration, switching after training to fast ODE integration for real-time control.
sections.details:
### IV-A Action Generation via Flow Matching
This method uses flow matching—continuously transporting probability density from a simple base distribution (such as a standard normal distribution) to the target action distribution—as an action generator. The evolution of intermediate action $X_t$ is governed by an ordinary differential equation (ODE: $dX_t = u_t(X_t)dt$), and a neural network is trained to learn this velocity vector field $u^\theta_t$.

Equally important is the interchangeability with stochastic differential equations (SDEs). Adding a diffusion term $\sigma_t dW_t$ alongside the score function (gradient of log probability density) as a correction term allows an SDE to trace the exact same marginal probability density path as the ODE. Remarkably, under the straight-line probability paths adopted here, the score function can be computed analytically directly from the learned vector field $u^\theta_t$, removing the need to train a separate score model.

### IV-B Offline Imitation Learning
When expert demonstrations are available, the model is first pretrained in an Actor-Critic framework. The actor network is trained to minimize both a vector field regression loss toward expert actions (BC loss) and a loss maximizing action values estimated by the critic network (Q loss).

### IV-C Online RL with SDE Exploration
During online interaction with the environment, deterministic ODE sampling provides insufficient exploration. The system therefore switches action sampling to an SDE:
- **Adaptive Noise Schedule**: A noise schedule $\sigma_t$ is designed to be large at early generation steps $t$ and decay toward the end, with its overall magnitude scaled by a learnable parameter $\alpha$.
- **Pathwise Surrogate Entropy**: Directly computing the action entropy (log density) of generative policies is mathematically intractable. Observing that discretizing the SDE via the Euler-Maruyama scheme yields a Gaussian conditional transition probability at each step, the authors introduce a "pathwise surrogate entropy" by summing the negative log-likelihood along the integration path. This enables maximum-entropy reinforcement learning without prohibitive computational costs.

As training progresses and parameter $\alpha$ decays toward zero, the SDE naturally collapses into a deterministic ODE. Consequently, during deployment and testing, noise-free ODE sampling over just a few integration steps delivers extremely fast, deterministic action outputs.

sections.heading: Unmatched Stability Under Harsh Disturbances: F1TENTH Validation
sections.summary: Testing on circular and figure-eight drift tasks in an F1TENTH digital twin showed that the proposed method achieved a 100% success rate even under extreme conditions (S5) combining parameter variations and disturbances, despite training solely on the nominal model. With a 0.5 ms inference latency, it significantly outperformed model-based baselines.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup and Disturbance Scenarios
Simulations ran at a 50 Hz control frequency (0.02 s time step). To test robustness, five evaluation scenarios (S1 to S5) were designed:
- **S1**: Nominal model without noise
- **S2**: Up to 20% error added to initial states
- **S3**: S2 plus random variations of ±20% in parameters like vehicle mass and moment of inertia
- **S4**: S3 plus integration noise and colored noise (OU process) injected into tire forces
- **S5**: S4 plus time-varying drifts in tire stiffness and road friction coefficient $\mu$ (the most severe condition)

Six controller variants were evaluated: the expert model-based controller (HDDC), offline imitation learning alone (Offline), and the proposed method using SDE generation and ODE generation (both fine-tuned and scratch-trained versions).

### V-B Drift Tracking Performance and Disturbance Robustness
In the nominal scenario (S1), all online-trained proposed variants achieved a 100% success rate (SR) across both circular and figure-eight tasks. In the most demanding disturbance scenario (S5), HDDC success plummeted to 68% in circular drift and 25% in figure-eight drift, while the Offline policy collapsed (17% and 2%). In contrast, the proposed method retained a 100% success rate across all configurations.

In trajectory accuracy, the proposed method reduced root-mean-square cross-track error $e_d$ by 37% to over 49% compared to HDDC, along with substantial tracking improvements in vehicle sideslip angle $\beta$ and velocity $v_x$. Notably, this exceptional robustness was achieved without any domain randomization during training—the policy trained exclusively on the nominal model. Stochastic exploration via SDE sampling exposed the policy to diverse handling-limit states, naturally inducing strong disturbance resistance.

### V-C Ablation Studies and Computational Speed
Compared against standard RL algorithms (SAC and PPO), SAC and PPO completely failed to learn drifting behaviors from scratch and could not complete complex tasks like figure-eight drifting even with pretraining. Additionally, training exclusively with an ODE (Flow-ODE) destabilized learning, confirming the necessity of SDE exploration.

Regarding the number of action generation integration steps $N$, $N=4$ proved sufficient for peak performance. On an Intel NUC (NUC13ANKi7), inference latency was only 0.5 ms—more than three times faster than HDDC (1.702 ms).

sections.heading: Generative RL Paving the Way for Driving at the Limit
sections.summary: This research establishes a new reinforcement learning framework using generative models as action policies. In an F1TENTH platform mimicking real hardware dynamics, it achieved autonomous drifting combining real-time execution, tight trajectory tracking, and robustness to disturbances.
sections.details:
This paper presented a generative policy reinforcement learning framework for autonomous vehicles operating at physical handling limits. By coupling a flow matching action generator with SDE-based adaptive exploration and surrogate entropy regularization, it enables stable online learning.

Experiments confirmed that both fine-tuning from expert demonstrations and learning completely from scratch acquire high-level circular and figure-eight drifting in short training periods. Furthermore, it demonstrated tracking accuracy and disturbance rejection superior to conventional model-based control and standard RL (SAC/PPO), operating with an ultra-low latency of 0.5 ms. These results vividly highlight generative AI as a powerful tool for end-to-end control of autonomous mobile robots in extreme conditions.

takeaways: Flow matching generative policies can capture multimodal action distributions, making them a more powerful alternative to conventional Gaussian policies in delicate continuous control tasks at handling limits.

An 'SDE-to-ODE' strategy—exploring stochastically with SDEs during training and sampling deterministically and quickly with ODEs during inference—is highly effective for balancing control performance with real-time requirements.

Using a 'pathwise surrogate entropy' based on discretized SDE transition probabilities bypasses intractable log-density evaluations in generative models, allowing straightforward implementation of maximum-entropy RL.

Experiencing diverse dynamic states during exploration naturally yields zero-shot robustness against severe parameter variations and disturbances without requiring explicit domain randomization during training.
limitations: Evaluations remain confined to the F1TENTH digital twin (a high-fidelity simulator); full physical validation accounting for tire thermal dynamics and local track roughness remains future work.

While increasing integration steps $N$ slightly improves precision, it increases backpropagation compute costs and risks gradient explosion, leaving reliance on step-number tuning and gradient clipping.
The observed performance gap relative to the model-based controller may vary depending on the parameter tuning of the baseline controller itself (such as HDDC used for expert demonstrations).
